I am retired and living on a fixed income. I don't want data about me used to charge me higher prices. I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

They’re calling it “personalized pricing,” but let’s be clear: What stores like Walmart are considering is a way to raise prices on people who the data says can afford it. And that money will go straight to their bottom line. It’s a way to use big data to make things even more expensive than they already are.

The rule that the FTC is currently considering would give corporations a green light to price gouge so long as they disclose that they’re doing it. That’s not good enough. Even if you think the wealthy should pay more, why should corporations be the ones who benefit? If you want the wealthy to pay more, tax the rich, and use the money for something useful to our society!
